blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Harry went down to breakfast next morning to find the three Dursleys already sitting around the kitchen table. They were watching a brand-new television, a welcome-home-for-the-summer present for Dudley, who had been complaining loudly about the long walk between the fridge and the television in the living room. Dudley had spent most of the summer in the kitchen, his piggy little eyes fixed on the screen and his five chins wobbling as he ate continually.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Harry sat down between Dudley and Uncle Vernon, a large, beefy man with very little neck and a lot of moustache. Far from wishing Harry a happy birthday, none of the Dursleys gave any sign that they had noticed Harry enter the room, but Harry was far too used to this to care. He helped himself to a piece of toast and then looked up at the newsreader on the television, who was halfway through a report on an escaped convict.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘… the public is warned that Black is armed and extremely dangerous. A special hotline has been set up, and any sighting of Black should be reported immediately.’

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘No need to tell us he’s no good,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: snorted Uncle Vernon, staring over the top of his newspaper at the prisoner.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘Look at the state of him, the filthy layabout! Look at his hair!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: He shot a nasty look sideways at Harry, whose untidy hair had always been a source of great annoyance to Uncle Vernon. Compared to the man on the television, however, whose gaunt face was surrounded by a matted, elbow-length tangle, Harry felt very well groomed indeed.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The newsreader had reappeared.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘The Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries will announce today –’

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘Hang on!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: barked Uncle Vernon, staring furiously at the newsreader.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘You didn’t tell us where that maniac’s escaped from! What use is that? Lunatic could be coming up the street right now!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Aunt Petunia, who was bony and horse-faced, whipped around and peered intently out of the kitchen window. Harry knew Aunt Petunia would simply love to be the one to call the hotline number. She was the nosiest woman in the world and spent most of her life spying on her boring, law-abiding neighbours.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘When will they learn,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Uncle Vernon, pounding the table with his large purple fist,

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘that hanging’s the only way to deal with these people?’

blocks.speaker: Aunt Petunia
blocks.text: ‘Very true,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Aunt Petunia, who was still squinting into next door’s runner-beans.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Uncle Vernon drained his teacup, glanced at his watch and added,

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘I’d better be off in a minute, Petunia, Marge’s train gets in at ten.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Harry, whose thoughts had been upstairs with the Broomstick Servicing Kit, was brought back to earth with an unpleasant bump.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Aunt Marge?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: he blurted out.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘Sh-she’s not coming here, is she?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Aunt Marge was Uncle Vernon’s sister. Even though she was not a blood relative of Harry’s (whose mother had been Aunt Petunia’s sister), he had been forced to call her ‘Aunt’ all his life. Aunt Marge lived in the country, in a house with a large garden, where she bred bulldogs. She didn’t often stay in Privet Drive, because she couldn’t bear to leave her precious dogs, but each of her visits stood out horribly vividly in Harry’s mind.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: At Dudley’s fifth birthday party, Aunt Marge had whacked Harry around the shins with her walking stick to stop him beating Dudley at musical statues. A few years later, she had turned up at Christmas with a computerised robot for Dudley and a box of dog biscuits for Harry. On her last visit, the year before Harry had started at Hogwarts, Harry had accidentally trodden on the paw of her favourite dog. Ripper had chased Harry out into the garden and up a tree, and Aunt Marge had refused to call him off until past midnight. The memory of this incident still brought tears of laughter to Dudley’s eyes.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘Marge’ll be here for a week,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Uncle Vernon snarled,

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘and while we’re on the subject,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: he pointed a fat finger threateningly at Harry,

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘we need to get a few things straight before I go and collect her.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Dudley smirked and withdrew his gaze from the television. Watching Harry being bullied by Uncle Vernon was Dudley’s favourite form of entertainment.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘Firstly,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: growled Uncle Vernon,

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘you’ll keep a civil tongue in your head when you’re talking to Marge.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘All right,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Harry bitterly, ‘if she does when she’s talking to me.’

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘Secondly,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Uncle Vernon, acting as though he had not heard Harry’s reply,

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘as Marge doesn’t know anything about your abnormality, I don’t want any – any funny stuff while she’s here. You behave yourself, got me?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘I will if she does,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Harry through gritted teeth.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘And thirdly,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Uncle Vernon, his mean little eyes now slits in his great purple face,

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘we’ve told Marge you attend St Brutus’s Secure Centre for Incurably Criminal Boys.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘What?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Harry yelled.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘And you’ll be sticking to that story, boy, or there’ll be trouble,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: spat Uncle Vernon.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Harry sat there, white-faced and furious, staring at Uncle Vernon, hardly able to believe it. Aunt Marge coming for a week-long visit – it was the worst birthday present the Dursleys had ever given him, including that pair of Uncle Vernon’s old socks.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘Well, Petunia,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Uncle Vernon, getting heavily to his feet,

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘I’ll be off to the station, then. Want to come along for the ride, Dudders?’

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘No,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Dudley, whose attention had returned to the television now that Uncle Vernon had finished threatening Harry.

blocks.speaker: Aunt Petunia
blocks.text: ‘Duddy’s got to make himself smart for his auntie,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Aunt Petunia, smoothing Dudley’s thick blond hair.

blocks.speaker: Aunt Petunia
blocks.text: ‘Mummy’s bought him a lovely new bow-tie.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Uncle Vernon clapped Dudley on his porky shoulder.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘See you in a bit, then,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: he said, and he left the kitchen.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Harry, who had been sitting in a kind of horrified trance, had a sudden idea. Abandoning his toast, he got quickly to his feet and followed Uncle Vernon to the front door.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Uncle Vernon was pulling on his car coat.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘I’m not taking you,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: he snarled, as he turned to see Harry watching him.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Like I wanted to come,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Harry coldly.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘I want to ask you something.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Uncle Vernon eyed him suspiciously.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘Third-years at Hog – at my school are allowed to visit the village sometimes,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Harry.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘So?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: snapped Uncle Vernon, taking his car keys from a hook next to the door.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘I need you to sign the permission form,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Harry in a rush.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘And why should I do that?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: sneered Uncle Vernon.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Well,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Harry, choosing his words carefully, ‘it’ll be hard work, pretending to Aunt Marge I go to that St Whatsits …’

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘St Brutus’s Secure Centre for Incurably Criminal Boys!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: bellowed Uncle Vernon, and Harry was pleased to hear a definite note of panic in Uncle Vernon’s voice.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘Exactly,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Harry, looking calmly up into Uncle Vernon’s large, purple face.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘It’s a lot to remember. I’ll have to make it sound convincing, won’t I? What if I accidentally let something slip?’

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘You’ll get the stuffing knocked out of you, won’t you?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: roared Uncle Vernon, advancing on Harry with his fist raised. But Harry stood his ground.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Knocking the stuffing out of me won’t make Aunt Marge forget what I could tell her,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: he said grimly.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Uncle Vernon stopped, his fist still raised, his face an ugly puce.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘But if you sign my permission form,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Harry went on quickly,

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘I swear I’ll remember where I’m supposed to go to school, and I’ll act like a Mug – like I’m normal and everything.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Harry could tell that Uncle Vernon was thinking it over, even if his teeth were bared and a vein was throbbing in his temple.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘Right,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: he snapped finally.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘I shall monitor your behaviour carefully during Marge’s visit. If, at the end of it, you’ve toed the line and kept to the story, I’ll sign your ruddy form.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: He wheeled around, pulled open the front door and slammed it so hard that one of the little panes of glass at the top fell out.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Harry didn’t return to the kitchen. He went back upstairs to his bedroom. If he was going to act like a real Muggle, he’d better start now. Slowly and sadly he gathered up all his presents and his birthday cards and hid them under the loose floorboard with his homework. Then he went to Hedwig’s cage. Errol seemed to have recovered; he and Hedwig were both asleep, heads under their wings. Harry sighed, then poked them both awake.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Hedwig,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: he said gloomily, ‘you’re going to have to clear off for a week. Go with Errol, Ron’ll look after you. I’ll write him a note, explaining. And don’t look at me like that’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: – Hedwig’s large amber eyes were reproachful, ‘it’s not my fault. It’s the only way I’ll be allowed to visit Hogsmeade with Ron and Hermione.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Ten minutes later, Errol and Hedwig (who had a note to Ron bound to her leg) soared out of the window and out of sight. Harry, now feeling thoroughly miserable, put the empty cage away inside the wardrobe.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: But Harry didn’t have long to brood. In next to no time, Aunt Petunia was shrieking up the stairs for Harry to come down and get ready to welcome their guest.

blocks.speaker: Aunt Petunia
blocks.text: ‘Do something about your hair!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Aunt Petunia snapped as he reached the hall.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Harry couldn’t see the point of trying to make his hair lie flat. Aunt Marge loved criticising him, so the untidier he looked, the happier she would be.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: All too soon, there was a crunch of gravel outside as Uncle Vernon’s car pulled back into the driveway, then the clunk of the car doors, and footsteps on the garden path.

blocks.speaker: Aunt Petunia
blocks.text: ‘Get the door!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Aunt Petunia hissed at Harry.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: A feeling of great gloom in his stomach, Harry pulled the door open.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: On the threshold stood Aunt Marge. She was very like Uncle Vernon; large, beefy and purple-faced, she even had a moustache, though not as bushy as his. In one hand she held an enormous suitcase, and tucked under the other was an old and evil-tempered bulldog.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Where’s my Dudders?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: roared Aunt Marge.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Where’s my neffy poo?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Dudley came waddling down the hall, his blond hair plastered flat to his fat head, a bow-tie just visible under his many chins. Aunt Marge thrust the suitcase into Harry’s stomach, knocking the wind out of him, seized Dudley in a tight one-armed hug and planted a large kiss on his cheek.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Harry knew perfectly well that Dudley only put up with Aunt Marge’s hugs because he was well paid for it, and sure enough, when they broke apart, Dudley had a crisp twenty-pound note clutched in his fat fist.

blocks.speaker: Aunt Petunia
blocks.text: ‘Petunia!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: shouted Aunt Marge, striding past Harry as though he was a hat-stand. Aunt Marge and Aunt Petunia kissed, or rather, Aunt Marge bumped her large jaw against Aunt Petunia’s bony cheekbone.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Uncle Vernon now came in, smiling jovially as he shut the door.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Tea, Marge?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: he said.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘And what will Ripper take?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Ripper can have some tea out of my saucer,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Aunt Marge, as they all trooped into the kitchen, leaving Harry alone in the hall with the suitcase. But Harry wasn’t complaining; any excuse not to be with Aunt Marge was fine by him, so he began to heave the case upstairs into the spare bedroom, taking as long as he could.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: By the time he got back to the kitchen, Aunt Marge had been supplied with tea and fruitcake and Ripper was lapping noisily in the corner. Harry saw Aunt Petunia wince slightly as specks of tea and drool flecked her clean floor. Aunt Petunia hated animals.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘Who’s looking after the other dogs, Marge?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Uncle Vernon asked.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Oh, I’ve got Colonel Fubster managing them,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: boomed Aunt Marge.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘He’s retired now, good for him to have something to do. But I couldn’t leave poor old Ripper. He pines if he’s away from me.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Ripper began to growl again as Harry sat down. This directed Aunt Marge’s attention to Harry for the first time.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘So!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: she barked.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Still here, are you?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Yes,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Harry.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Don’t you say “yes” in that ungrateful tone,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Aunt Marge growled.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘It’s damn good of Vernon and Petunia to keep you. Wouldn’t have done it myself. You’d have gone straight to an orphanage if you’d been dumped on my doorstep.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Harry was bursting to say that he’d rather live in an orphanage than with the Dursleys, but the thought of the Hogsmeade form stopped him. He forced his face into a painful smile.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Don’t you smirk at me!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: boomed Aunt Marge.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘I can see you haven’t improved since I last saw you. I hoped school would knock some manners into you.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: She took a large gulp of tea, wiped her moustache and said, ‘Where is it that you send him, again, Vernon?’

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘St Brutus’s,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Uncle Vernon promptly.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘It’s a first-rate institution for hopeless cases.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘I see,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Aunt Marge.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Do they use the cane at St Brutus’s, boy?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: she barked across the table.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘Er –’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Uncle Vernon nodded curtly behind Aunt Marge’s back.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘Yes,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Harry. Then, feeling he might as well do the thing properly, he added, ‘All the time.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Excellent,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Aunt Marge.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘I won’t have this namby-pamby, wishy-washy nonsense about not hitting people who deserve it. A good thrashing is what’s needed in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred. Have you been beaten often?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Oh, yeah,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Harry, ‘loads of times.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Aunt Marge narrowed her eyes.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘I still don’t like your tone, boy,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: she said.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘If you can speak of your beatings in that casual way, they clearly aren’t hitting you hard enough. Petunia, I’d write if I were you. Make it clear that you approve the use of extreme force in this boy’s case.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Perhaps Uncle Vernon was worried that Harry might forget their bargain; in any case, he changed the subject abruptly.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘Heard the news this morning, Marge? What about that escaped prisoner, eh?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: As Aunt Marge started to make herself at home, Harry caught himself thinking almost longingly of life at number four without her. Uncle Vernon and Aunt Petunia usually encouraged Harry to stay out of their way, which Harry was only too happy to do. Aunt Marge, on the other hand, wanted Harry under her eye at all times, so that she could boom out suggestions for his improvement. She delighted in comparing Harry with Dudley, and took huge pleasure in buying Dudley expensive presents while glaring at Harry, as though daring him to ask why he hadn’t got a present too. She also kept throwing out dark hints about what made Harry such an unsatisfactory person.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘You mustn’t blame yourself for the way the boy’s turned out, Vernon,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: she said over lunch on the third day.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘If there’s something rotten on the inside, there’s nothing anyone can do about it.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Harry tried to concentrate on his food, but his hands shook and his face was starting to burn with anger. Remember the form, he told himself. Think about Hogsmeade. Don’t say anything. Don’t rise –

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Aunt Marge reached for her glass of wine.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘It’s one of the basic rules of breeding,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: she said.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘You see it all the time with dogs. If there’s something wrong with the bitch, there’ll be something wrong with the pup –’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: At that moment, the wine glass Aunt Marge was holding exploded in her hand. Shards of glass flew in every direction and Aunt Marge spluttered and blinked, her great ruddy face dripping.

blocks.speaker: Aunt Petunia
blocks.text: ‘Marge!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: squealed Aunt Petunia.

blocks.speaker: Aunt Petunia
blocks.text: ‘Marge, are you all right?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Not to worry,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: grunted Aunt Marge, mopping her face with her napkin.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘Must have squeezed it too hard. Did the same thing at Colonel Fubster’s the other day. No need to fuss, Petunia, I have a very firm grip …’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: But Aunt Petunia and Uncle Vernon were both looking at Harry suspiciously, so he decided he’d better skip pudding and escape from the table as soon as he could.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Outside in the hall, he leant against the wall, breathing deeply. It had been a long time since he’d lost control and made something explode. He couldn’t afford to let it happen again. The Hogsmeade form wasn’t the only thing at stake – if he carried on like that, he’d be in trouble with the Ministry of Magic.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Harry was still an underage wizard, and he was forbidden by wizard law to do magic outside school. His record wasn’t exactly clean, either. Only last summer he’d got an official warning which had stated quite clearly that if the Ministry got wind of any more magic in Privet Drive, Harry would face expulsion from Hogwarts.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: He heard the Dursleys leaving the table and hurried upstairs out of the way. *

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Harry got through the next three days by forcing himself to think about his Handbook of Do-it-Yourself Broomcare whenever Aunt Marge started on him. This worked quite well, though it seemed to give him a glazed look, because Aunt Marge started voicing the opinion that he was mentally subnormal.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: At last, at long last, the final evening of Marge’s stay arrived. Aunt Petunia cooked a fancy dinner and Uncle Vernon uncorked several bottles of wine. They got all the way through the soup and the salmon without a single mention of Harry’s faults; during the lemon meringue pie, Uncle Vernon bored them all with a long talk about Grunnings, his drill-making company; then Aunt Petunia made coffee and Uncle Vernon brought out a bottle of brandy.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Can I tempt you, Marge?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Aunt Marge had already had rather a lot of wine. Her huge face was very red.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Just a small one, then,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: she chuckled.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘A bit more than that … and a bit more … that’s the boy.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Dudley was eating his fourth slice of pie. Aunt Petunia was sipping coffee with her little finger sticking out. Harry really wanted to disappear into his bedroom, but he met Uncle Vernon’s angry little eyes and knew he would have to sit it out.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘Aah,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Aunt Marge, smacking her lips and putting the empty brandy glass back down.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Excellent nosh, Petunia. It’s normally just a fry-up for me of an evening, with twelve dogs to look after …’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: She burped richly and patted her great tweed stomach.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Pardon me. But I do like to see a healthy-sized boy,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: she went on, winking at Dudley.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘You’ll be a proper-sized man, Dudders, like your father. Yes, I’ll have a spot more brandy, Vernon …’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Now, this one here –’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: She jerked her head at Harry, who felt his stomach clench. The Handbook, he thought quickly.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘This one’s got a mean, runty look about him. You get that with dogs. I had Colonel Fubster drown one last year. Ratty little thing it was. Weak. Underbred.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Harry was trying to remember page twelve of his book: A Charm to Cure Reluctant Reversers.

blocks.speaker: Aunt Petunia
blocks.text: ‘It all comes down to blood, as I was saying the other day. Bad blood will out. Now, I’m saying nothing against your family, Petunia’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: – she patted Aunt Petunia’s bony hand with her shovel-like one,

blocks.speaker: Aunt Petunia
blocks.text: ‘but your sister was a bad egg. They turn up in the best families. Then she ran off with a wastrel and here’s the result right in front of us.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Harry was staring at his plate, a funny ringing in his ears. Grasp your broom firmly by the tail, he thought. But he couldn’t remember what came next. Aunt Marge’s voice seemed to be boring into him like one of Uncle Vernon’s drills.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘This Potter,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Aunt Marge loudly, seizing the brandy bottle and splashing more into her glass and over the tablecloth,

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘you never told me what he did?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Uncle Vernon and Aunt Petunia were looking extremely tense. Dudley had even looked up from his pie to gape at his parents.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘He – didn’t work,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Uncle Vernon, with half a glance at Harry.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘Unemployed.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘As I expected!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Aunt Marge, taking a huge swig of brandy and wiping her chin on her sleeve.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘A no-account, good-for-nothing, lazy scrounger who –’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘He was not,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Harry suddenly. The table went very quiet. Harry was shaking all over. He had never felt so angry in his life.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘MORE BRANDY!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: yelled Uncle Vernon, who had gone very white. He emptied the bottle into Aunt Marge’s glass.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘You, boy,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: he snarled at Harry.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘Go to bed, go on –’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘No, Vernon,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: hiccoughed Aunt Marge, holding up a hand, her tiny bloodshot eyes fixed on Harry’s.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘Go on, boy, go on. Proud of your parents, are you? They go and get themselves killed in a car crash (drunk, I expect) –’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘They didn’t die in a car crash!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Harry, who found himself on his feet.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘They died in a car crash, you nasty little liar, and left you to be a burden on their decent, hardworking relatives!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: screamed Aunt Marge, swelling with fury.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘You are an insolent, ungrateful little –’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: But Aunt Marge suddenly stopped speaking. For a moment, it looked as though words had failed her. She seemed to be swelling with inexpressible anger – but the swelling didn’t stop. Her great red face started to expand, her tiny eyes bulged and her mouth stretched too tightly for speech. Next second, several buttons burst from her tweed jacket and pinged off the walls – she was inflating like a monstrous balloon, her stomach bursting free of her tweed waistband, each of her fingers blowing up like a salami …

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘MARGE!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: yelled Uncle Vernon and Aunt Petunia together, as Aunt Marge’s whole body began to rise off her chair towards the ceiling. She was entirely round, now, like a vast life buoy with piggy eyes, and her hands and feet stuck out weirdly as she drifted up into the air, making apoplectic popping noises. Ripper came skidding into the room, barking madly.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘NOOOOOOO!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Uncle Vernon seized one of Marge’s feet and tried to pull her down again, but was almost lifted from the floor himself. Next second, Ripper had leapt forward and sunk his teeth into Uncle Vernon’s leg.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Harry tore from the dining room before anyone could stop him, heading for the cupboard under the stairs. The cupboard door burst magically open as he reached it. In seconds, he had heaved his trunk to the front door. He sprinted upstairs and threw himself under the bed, wrenched up the loose floorboard and grabbed the pillowcase full of his books and birthday presents. He wriggled out, seized Hedwig’s empty cage and dashed back downstairs to his trunk, just as Uncle Vernon burst out of the dining room, his trouser leg in bloody tatters.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘COME BACK IN HERE!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: he bellowed.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘COME BACK AND PUT HER RIGHT!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: But a reckless rage had come over Harry. He kicked his trunk open, pulled out his wand and pointed it at Uncle Vernon.

blocks.speaker: Uncle Vernon
blocks.text: ‘She deserved it,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Harry said, breathing very fast.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘She deserved what she got. You keep away from me.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: He fumbled behind him for the catch on the door.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘I’m going,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Harry said.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: ‘I’ve had enough.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: And next moment, he was out in the dark, quiet street, heaving his heavy trunk behind him, Hedwig’s cage under his arm.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban - Chapter 1 - The Riddle House —

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The villagers of Little Hangleton still called it ‘the Riddle House’, even though it had been many years since the Riddle family had lived there. It stood on a hill overlooking the village, some of its windows boarded, tiles missing from its roof, and ivy spreading unchecked over its face. Once a fine‑looking manor, and easily the largest and grandest building for miles around, the Riddle House was now damp, derelict and unoccupied.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The Little Hangletons all agreed that the old house was ‘creepy’. Half a century ago, something strange and horrible had happened there, something that the older inhabitants of the village still liked to discuss when topics for gossip were scarce. The story had been picked over so many times, and had been embroidered in so many places, that nobody was quite sure what the truth was any more. Every version of the tale, however, started in the same place: fifty years before, at daybreak on a fine summer’s morning, when the Riddle House had still been well kept and impressive, and a maid had entered the drawing room to find all three Riddles dead. The maid had run screaming down the hill into the village, and roused as many people as she could.

blocks.speaker: Barwoman
blocks.text: ‘Who else had a key to the back door, then?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: barked the cook.

blocks.speaker: Cook
blocks.text: ‘There’s been a spare key hanging in the gardener’s cottage far back as I can remember! Nobody forced the door last night! No broken windows! All Frank had to do was creep up to the big house while we was all sleeping …’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The villagers exchanged dark looks.

blocks.speaker: Man at the bar
blocks.text: ‘I always thought he had a nasty look about him, right enough,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: grunted a man at the bar.

blocks.speaker: Landlord
blocks.text: ‘War turned him funny, if you ask me,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said the landlord.

blocks.speaker: Excited Woman
blocks.text: ‘Told you I wouldn’t like to get on the wrong side of Frank, didn’t I, Dot?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said an excited woman in the corner.

blocks.speaker: Dot
blocks.text: ‘Horrible temper,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Dot, nodding fervently,

blocks.speaker: Dot
blocks.text: ‘I remember, when he was a kid …’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: By the following morning, hardly anyone in Little Hangleton doubted that Frank Bryce had killed the Riddles.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: But over in the neighbouring town of Great Hangleton, in the dark and dingy police station, Frank was stubbornly repeating, again and again, that he was innocent, and that the only person he had seen near the house on the day of the Riddles’ deaths had been a teenage boy, a stranger, dark‑haired and pale. Nobody else in the village had seen any such boy, and the police were quite sure that Frank had invented him.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Then, just when things were looking very serious for Frank, the report on the Riddles’ bodies came back and changed everything.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The police had never read an odder report. A team of doctors had examined the bodies, and had concluded that none of the Riddles had been poisoned, stabbed, shot, strangled, suffocated or (as far as they could tell) harmed at all. In fact, the report continued, in a tone of unmistakable bewilderment, the Riddles all appeared to be in perfect health – apart from the fact that they were all dead. The doctors did note (as though determined to find something wrong with the bodies) that each of the Riddles had a look of terror upon his or her face – but as the frustrated police said, whoever heard of three people being frightened to death?

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: As there was no proof that the Riddles had been murdered at all, the police were forced to let Frank go. The Riddles were buried in the Little Hangleton churchyard, and their graves remained objects of curiosity for a while. To everyone’s surprise, and amidst a cloud of suspicion, Frank Bryce returned to his cottage in the grounds of the Riddle House.

blocks.speaker: Dot
blocks.text: ‘S’far as I’m concerned, he killed them, and I don’t care what the police say,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Dot in the Hanged Man.

blocks.speaker: Dot
blocks.text: ‘And if he had any decency, he’d leave here, knowing as how we knows he did it.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: But Frank did not leave. He stayed to tend the garden for the next family who lived in the Riddle House, and then the next – for neither family stayed long. Perhaps it was partly because of Frank that each new owner said there was a nasty feeling about the place, which, in the absence of inhabitants, started to fall into disrepair. *

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The wealthy man who owned the Riddle House these days neither lived there nor put it to any use; they said in the village that he kept it for ‘tax reasons’, though nobody was very clear what these might be. The wealthy owner continued to pay Frank to do the gardening, however. Frank was nearing his seventy-seventh birthday now, very deaf, his bad leg stiffer than ever, but could be seen pottering around the flowerbeds in fine weather, even though the weeds were starting to creep up on him.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Weeds were not the only things Frank had to contend with, either. Boys from the village made a habit of throwing stones through the windows of the Riddle House. They rode their bicycles over the lawns Frank worked so hard to keep smooth. Once or twice, they broke into the old house for a dare. They knew that old Frank was devoted to the house and grounds, and it amused them to see him limping across the garden, brandishing his stick and yelling croakily at them. Frank, on his part, believed the boys tormented him because they, like their parents and grandparents, thought him a murderer. So when Frank awoke one night in August, and saw something very odd up at the old house, he merely assumed that the boys had gone one step further in their attempts to punish him.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: It was Frank’s bad leg that woke him; it was paining him worse than ever in his old age. He got up and limped downstairs into the kitchen, with the idea of re-filling his hot-water bottle to ease the stiffness in his knee. Standing at the sink, filling the kettle, he looked up at the Riddle House and saw lights glimmering in its upper windows. Frank knew at once what was going on. The boys had broken into the house again, and judging by the flickering quality of the light, they had started a fire.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Frank had no telephone, and in any case, he had deeply mistrusted the police ever since they had taken him in for questioning about the Riddles’ deaths. He put down the kettle at once, hurried back upstairs as fast as his bad leg would allow, and was soon back in his kitchen, fully dressed and removing a rusty old key from its hook by the door. He picked up his walking stick, which was propped against the wall, and set off into the night.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The front door of the Riddle House bore no sign of being forced, and nor did any of the windows. Frank limped around to the back of the house until he reached a door almost completely hidden by ivy, took out the old key, put it into the lock and opened the door noiselessly.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: He had let himself into the cavernous kitchen. Frank had not entered it for many years; nevertheless, although it was very dark, he remembered where the door into the hall was, and he groped his way towards it, his nostrils full of the smell of decay, ears pricked for any sound of footsteps or voices from overhead. He reached the hall, which was a little lighter owing to the large mullioned windows either side of the front door, and started to climb the stairs, blessing the dust which lay thick upon the stone, because it muffled the sound of his feet and stick.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: On the landing, Frank turned right, and saw at once where the intruders were: at the very end of the passage a door stood ajar, and a flickering light shone through the gap, casting a long sliver of gold across the black floor. Frank edged closer and closer, grasping his walking stick firmly. Several feet from the entrance, he was able to see a narrow slice of the room beyond.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The fire, he now saw, had been lit in the grate. This surprised him. He stopped moving and listened intently, for a man’s voice spoke within the room; it sounded timid and fearful.

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘There is a little more in the bottle, my Lord, if you are still hungry.’

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘Later,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said a second voice. This, too, belonged to a man – but it was strangely high-pitched, and cold as a sudden blast of icy wind. Something about that voice made the sparse hairs on the back of Frank’s neck stand up.

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘Move me closer to the fire, Wormtail.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Frank turned his right ear towards the door, the better to hear. There came the chink of a bottle being put down upon some hard surface, and then the dull scraping noise of a heavy chair being dragged across the floor. Frank caught a glimpse of a small man, his back to the door, pushing the chair into place. He was wearing a long black cloak, and there was a bald patch at the back of his head. Then he disappeared from sight again.

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘Where is Nagini?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said the cold voice.

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘I – I don’t know, my Lord,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said the first voice nervously.

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘She set out to explore the house, I think …’

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘You will milk her before we retire, Wormtail,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said the second voice.

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘I will need feeding in the night. The journey has tired me greatly.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Brow furrowed, Frank inclined his good ear still closer to the door, listening very hard. There was a pause, and then the man called Wormtail spoke again.

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘My Lord, may I ask how long we are going to stay here?’

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘A week,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said the cold voice.

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘Perhaps longer. The place is moderately comfortable, and the plan cannot proceed yet. It would be foolish to act before the Quidditch World Cup is over.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Frank inserted a gnarled finger into his ear and rotated it. Owing, no doubt, to a build-up of earwax, he had heard the word ‘Quidditch’, which was not a word at all.

blocks.speaker: Frank Bryce
blocks.text: ‘The – the Quidditch World Cup, my Lord?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Wormtail. (Frank dug his finger still more vigorously into his ear.)

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘Forgive me, but – I do not understand – why should we wait until the World Cup is over?’

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘Because, fool, at this very moment wizards are pouring into the country from all over the world, and every meddler from the Ministry of Magic will be on duty, on the watch for signs of unusual activity, checking and double-checking identities. They will be obsessed with security, lest the Muggles notice anything. So we wait.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Frank stopped trying to clear his ear out. He had distinctly heard the words ‘Ministry of Magic’,

blocks.speaker: Frank Bryce
blocks.text: ‘wizards’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: and ‘Muggles’. Plainly, each of these expressions meant something secret, and Frank could think of only two sorts of people who would speak in code – spies and criminals. Frank tightened his hold on his walking stick once more, and listened more closely still.

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘Your Lordship is still determined, then?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Wormtail said quietly.

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘Certainly I am determined, Wormtail.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: There was a note of menace in the cold voice now. A slight pause followed – and then Wormtail spoke, the words tumbling from him in a rush, as though he was forcing himself to say this before he lost his nerve.

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘It could be done without Harry Potter, my Lord.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Another pause, more protracted, and then –

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘Without Harry Potter?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: breathed the second voice softly.

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘I see …’

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘My Lord, I do not say this out of concern for the boy!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Wormtail, his voice rising squeakily.

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘The boy is nothing to me, nothing at all! It is merely that if we were to use another witch or wizard – any wizard – the thing could be done so much more quickly! If you allowed me to leave you for a short while – you know that I can disguise myself most effectively – I could be back here in as little as two days with a suitable person –’

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘I could use another wizard,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said the second voice softly,

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘that is true …’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Wormtail, sounding thoroughly relieved now,

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘My Lord, it makes sense,’

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘laying hands on Harry Potter would be so difficult, he is so well protected –’

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘And so you volunteer to go and fetch me a substitute? I wonder … perhaps the task of nursing me has become wearisome for you, Wormtail? Could this suggestion of abandoning the plan be nothing more than an attempt to desert me?’

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘My Lord! I – I have no wish to leave you, none at all –’

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘Do not lie to me!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: hissed the second voice.

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘I can always tell, Wormtail! You are regretting that you ever returned to me. I revolt you. I see you flinch when you look at me, feel you shudder when you touch me …’

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘No! My devotion to your Lordship –’

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘Your devotion is nothing more than cowardice. You would not be here if you had anywhere else to go. How am I to survive without you, when I need feeding every few hours? Who is to milk Nagini?’

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘But you seem so much stronger, my Lord –’

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘Liar,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: breathed the second voice.

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘I am no stronger, and a few days alone would be enough to rob me of the little health I have regained under your clumsy care. Silence!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Wormtail, who had been spluttering incoherently, fell silent at once. For a few seconds, Frank could hear nothing but the fire crackling. Then the second man spoke once more, in a whisper that was almost a hiss.

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘I have my reasons for using the boy, as I have already explained to you, and I will use no other. I have waited thirteen years. A few more months will make no difference. As for the protection surrounding the boy, I believe my plan will be effective. All that is needed is a little courage from you, Wormtail – courage you will find, unless you wish to feel the full extent of Lord Voldemort’s wrath –’

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘My Lord, I must speak!’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Wormtail, panic in his voice now.

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘All through our journey I have gone over the plan in my head – my Lord, Bertha Jorkins’s disappearance will not go unnoticed for long, and if we proceed, if I curse –’

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘If?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: whispered the second voice.

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘If? If you follow the plan, Wormtail, the Ministry need never know that anyone else has disappeared. You will do it quietly, and without fuss; I only wish that I could do it myself, but in my present condition … come, Wormtail, one more obstacle removed and our path to Harry Potter is clear. I am not asking you to do it alone. By that time, my faithful servant will have rejoined us –’

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘I am a faithful servant,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Wormtail, the merest trace of sullenness in his voice.

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘Wormtail, I need somebody with brains, somebody whose loyalty has never wavered, and you, unfortunately, fulfil neither requirement.’

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘I found you,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Wormtail, and there was definitely a sulky edge to his voice now.

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘I was the one who found you. I brought you Bertha Jorkins.’

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘That is true,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said the second man, sounding amused.

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘A stroke of brilliance I would not have thought possible from you, Wormtail – though, if truth be told, you were not aware how useful she would be when you caught her, were you?’

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘I – I thought she might be useful, my Lord –’

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘Liar,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said the second voice again, the cruel amusement more pronounced than ever.

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘However, I do not deny that her information was invaluable. Without it, I could never have formed our plan, and for that, you will have your reward, Wormtail. I will allow you to perform an essential task for me, one that many of my followers would give their right hands to perform …’

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘R-really, my Lord? What –?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Wormtail sounded terrified again.

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘Ah, Wormtail, you don’t want me to spoil the surprise? Your part will come at the very end … but I promise you, you will have the honour of being just as useful as Bertha Jorkins.’

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘You … you …’

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘You … are going … to kill me, too?’

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘Wormtail, Wormtail,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said the cold voice silkily,

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘why would I kill you? I killed Bertha because I had to. She was fit for nothing after my questioning, quite useless. In any case, awkward questions would have been asked if she had gone back to the Ministry with the news that she had met you on her holidays. Wizards who are supposed to be dead would do well not to run into Ministry of Magic witches at wayside inns …’

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: Wormtail muttered something so quietly that Frank could not hear it, but it made the second man laugh – an entirely mirthless laugh, cold as his speech.

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘We could have modified her memory? But Memory Charms can be broken by a powerful wizard, as I proved when I questioned her. It would be an insult to her memory not to use the information I extracted from her, Wormtail.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Out in the corridor, Frank suddenly became aware that the hand gripping his walking stick was slippery with sweat. The man with the cold voice had killed a woman. He was talking about it without any kind of remorse – with amusement. He was dangerous – a madman. And he was planning more murders – this boy, Harry Potter, whoever he was – was in danger –

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Frank knew what he must do. Now, if ever, was the time to go to the police. He would creep out of the house and head straight for the telephone box in the village … but the cold voice was speaking again, and Frank remained where he was, frozen to the spot, listening with all his might.

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘One more curse … my faithful servant at Hogwarts … Harry Potter is as good as mine, Wormtail. It is decided. There will be no more argument. But quiet … I think I hear Nagini …’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: And the second man’s voice changed. He started making noises such as Frank had never heard before; he was hissing and spitting without drawing breath. Frank thought he must be having some sort of fit or seizure. And then Frank heard movement behind him in the dark passageway. He turned to look behind him, and found himself paralysed with fright.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Something was slithering towards him along the dark corridor floor, and as it drew nearer to the sliver of firelight, he realised with a thrill of terror that it was a gigantic snake, at least twelve feet long. Horrified, transfixed, Frank stared at it as its undulating body cut a wide, curving track through the thick dust on the floor, coming closer and closer – what was he to do? The only means of escape was into the room where two men sat plotting murder, yet if he stayed where he was the snake would surely kill him –

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: But before he had made his decision, the snake was level with him, and then, incredibly, miraculously, it was passing; it was following the spitting, hissing noises made by the cold voice beyond the door, and in seconds, the tip of its diamond-patterned tail had vanished through the gap.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: There was sweat on Frank’s forehead now, and the hand on the walking stick was trembling. Inside the room, the cold voice was continuing to hiss, and Frank was visited by a strange idea, an impossible idea … This man could talk to snakes. Frank didn’t understand what was going on. He wanted more than anything to be back in his bed with his hot-water bottle. The problem was that his legs didn’t seem to want to move. As he stood there shaking, and trying to master himself, the cold voice switched abruptly to English again.

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘Nagini has interesting news, Wormtail,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: it said.

blocks.speaker: Wormtail
blocks.text: ‘In-indeed, my Lord?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said Wormtail.

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘Indeed, yes,’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said the voice.

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘According to Nagini, there is an old Muggle standing right outside this room, listening to every word we say.’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Frank didn’t have a chance to hide himself. There were footsteps, and then the door of the room was flung wide open. A short, balding man with greying hair, a pointed nose and small, watery eyes stood before Frank, a mixture of fear and alarm on his face.

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘Invite him inside, Wormtail. Where are your manners?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The cold voice was coming from the ancient armchair before the fire, but Frank couldn’t see the speaker. The snake, on the other hand, was curled up on the rotting hearth-rug, like some horrible travesty of a pet dog. Wormtail beckoned Frank into the room. Though still deeply shaken, Frank took a firmer grip upon his walking stick, and limped over the threshold.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The fire was the only source of light in the room; it was casting long, spidery shadows upon the walls. Frank stared at the back of the armchair; the man inside it seemed to be even smaller than his servant, for Frank couldn’t even see the back of his head.

blocks.speaker: Voldemort
blocks.text: ‘You heard everything, Muggle?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: said the cold voice.

blocks.speaker: Frank Bryce
blocks.text: ‘What’s that you’re calling me?’

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Slowly, with his face screwed up, as though he would rather have done anything than approach his master and the hearth-rug where the snake lay, the small man walked forwards and began to turn the chair. The snake lifted its ugly triangular head and hissed slightly as the legs of the chair snagged on its rug.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: And then the chair was facing Frank, and he saw what was sitting in it. His walking stick fell to the floor with a clatter. He opened his mouth and let out a scream. He was screaming so loudly that he never heard the words the thing in the chair spoke, as it raised a wand. There was a flash of green light, a rushing sound, and Frank Bryce crumpled. He was dead before he hit the floor.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Two hundred miles away, the boy called Harry Potter woke with a start.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You and Lucy, standing together outside the school. You turn the screen toward her.

blocks.speaker: Protagonist
blocks.text: "Do you remember this?"

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: She looks at the photograph.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "Of course I do. That was last month."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You shake your head.

blocks.speaker: Protagonist
blocks.text: "That was the last picture we took together. It was a year ago."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Lucy's smile fades. She takes the phone from your hand and examines the date. Her face goes pale.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "That's impossible."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You pull the phone back and open the calendar. The date is correct.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: A full year has passed since Lucy disappeared.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: But to her, barely an hour has gone by. Neither of you speaks.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Then Lucy notices something on the screen. Your battery is almost dead. She pulls out her own phone. The display lights up. The date is the same as yours.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: But the time is different. Not by a few minutes. By exactly fifty-nine minutes. You compare the two screens.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: For a moment, the only sound is the faint buzzing of your flashlight.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Then Lucy whispers something that makes your stomach drop.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "I remember the clouds."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You look at her.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "What clouds?"

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "The dark ones. They appeared while I was walking home."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: She swallows.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "And then I heard that sound."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The same roar. The same impossible sound that had shaken the school windows. Lucy looks down the corridor.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "I ran back inside. I thought something was happening outside."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You step closer to her.

blocks.speaker: Protagonist
blocks.text: "Then how did you get here?"

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "I don't know."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: She looks at the classroom doors.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "I opened my eyes, and I was standing here."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Suddenly, a bell rings. Both of you jump.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The sound echoes through the building, loud and metallic. You turn toward the main entrance.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The door that refused to move moments ago is now standing slightly open.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: A thin strip of pale light shines through the gap. You and Lucy exchange a glance. Then you walk toward it. Together. You push the door open. And stop.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Outside, there is no road. No buildings. No trees.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The entire school grounds have disappeared.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Beyond the entrance stretches an endless field of grey mist, illuminated by a pale, colourless sky.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The school stands alone in the middle of nothing. You step back inside. Lucy grips your arm.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "Where are we?"

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You don't answer. Because for the first time since this began, you realise something worse than being trapped. You might not be anywhere at all.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You return to the main corridor.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Lucy keeps looking over her shoulder, as though expecting someone to emerge from the classrooms. You decide to search the school.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: There has to be an explanation. A broken power supply. Some kind of gas leak. Maybe you're both unconscious somewhere, dreaming the same nightmare.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Anything is better than the alternative.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You check the principal's office first. The door is unlocked.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Inside, papers are scattered across the desk. A chair lies on its side. The computer monitor is dark.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You move the flashlight across the wall.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: A clock hangs above the filing cabinet. Its hands are frozen at 3:17. You check your phone. 3:17.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Lucy's phone displays the same time now. You look at the clock again. Its second hand begins to move. One tick. Then another.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The fluorescent light above the desk flickers on. A printer starts running by itself.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You and Lucy stare at it as a single sheet of paper slowly emerges. You walk over and pick it up. It's an attendance sheet. Today's date is printed at the top.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Below it are the names of every student in your class. You scan the list. Your name is there. Lucy's name is there, too.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: But beside both names, someone has written the same word. PRESENT. You turn the sheet over.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: On the back, written in thick black ink, are four words. DO NOT RING THE BELL.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: A bell rings somewhere in the building. Once. Twice. Three times. The lights go out.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: From the corridor comes the sound of hundreds of students talking.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Footsteps rush past the office door. Someone laughs.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: A teacher shouts for everyone to get back to class.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: For a brief moment, the school sounds exactly as it did before everyone vanished. Lucy looks toward the doorway.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "Can you hear them?"

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You nod. Then you hear your own voice among the crowd. Not your current voice. Your voice from an hour ago. Laughing. Talking. Walking through the school gate.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You slowly approach the office door.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Through the narrow window, you see students passing by.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: They're moving normally, carrying bags and chatting with their friends. Then you see yourself. Walking down the corridor.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The same clothes. The same backpack. The same expression you wore before the sky turned dark.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Your past self walks directly past the office.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: And behind you, walking toward the school gate, is Lucy. She looks exactly as she does now. Lucy grabs your shoulder.

blocks.speaker: Protagonist
blocks.text: "That's me."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: On the other side of the glass, your past self stops walking.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You watch as he looks up at the dark clouds. Then he runs toward the entrance. The image flickers.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The corridor outside becomes empty again. The voices stop. The lights remain off. You turn toward Lucy. She is staring at the window.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Tears are running down her face.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "I remember this."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You wait.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "I remember seeing you run inside. I thought you were scared of the storm."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: She wipes her eyes.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "Then I heard the roar. Everything went black."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: She looks at you.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "And then I was here."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You glance at the attendance sheet. PRESENT. Both of you.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: As though the school has been waiting for you to arrive.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: As though it knows exactly where you belong. ________________

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: A crackling sound comes from the loudspeaker above the office door. You freeze.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The school's announcement system hasn't worked since the lights went out.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Static fills the corridor. Then a familiar voice speaks. It's the principal.

blocks.speaker: Principal
blocks.text: "Attention, students."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The voice is distorted, as though coming from a damaged recording.

blocks.speaker: Principal
blocks.text: "Please proceed to your assigned classrooms."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You and Lucy remain still. The announcement repeats.

blocks.speaker: Principal
blocks.text: "Please proceed to your assigned classrooms."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Then the voice changes. It becomes quieter. Almost a whisper.

blocks.speaker: Principal
blocks.text: "Lucy?"

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: She stops breathing for a moment. The speaker crackles.

blocks.speaker: Principal
blocks.text: "Lucy, please report to the principal's office."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You look at her. She shakes her head.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "I don't want to."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: A long burst of static fills the air. Then the principal's voice returns.

blocks.speaker: Principal
blocks.text: "Lucy, your parents are waiting."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Lucy backs away from the speaker.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: “No.”

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The announcement continues.

blocks.speaker: Principal
blocks.text: “They have been waiting for one year.”

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You stare at Lucy. She looks just as terrified as you feel. The loudspeaker clicks off.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: For several seconds, neither of you moves.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Then a phone rings somewhere inside the office. You turn toward the desk. Your phone is in your hand. Lucy's phone is in her pocket.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The ringing comes from the dark computer beneath the desk. You crouch down.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: An old landline phone sits beside a stack of files. Its display is glowing.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The caller ID reads: LUCY'S HOME.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Lucy steps closer.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "That's my house."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The phone keeps ringing. You pick up the receiver.

blocks.speaker: Protagonist
blocks.text: "Hello?"

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: For a moment, there is only static. Then a woman's voice speaks.

blocks.speaker: Lucy's Mother
blocks.text: "Lucy?"

blocks.speaker: Lucy's Mother
blocks.text: "Lucy, sweetheart, where are you?"

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Lucy reaches for the receiver. You hand it to her.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "Mum?"

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: A sharp breath comes through the line.

blocks.speaker: Lucy's Mother
blocks.text: "Oh, thank God."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Lucy's mother begins crying.

blocks.speaker: Lucy's Mother
blocks.text: "Where have you been? We've been looking for you everywhere."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Lucy presses the receiver against her ear.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "Mum, I don't understand. I was only gone for an hour."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Silence.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Then her mother whispers:

blocks.speaker: Lucy's Mother
blocks.text: "Lucy, you've been missing for a year."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Lucy drops the receiver. It swings from the cord, knocking against the desk. You look at her. She looks at you.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Neither of you needs to say anything. The phone line goes dead.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Then, from somewhere deep inside the school, comes the sound of a classroom door opening. A chair scraping across the floor.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: And a teacher calling for attendance. ________________ You grab Lucy's hand.

blocks.speaker: Protagonist
blocks.text: "We need to leave."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You run toward the main entrance. This time, the door opens easily.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Beyond it, the endless grey field is gone. The road is back. The buildings are back.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The trees stand motionless beneath the dark sky.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: But the streets are completely empty. You step outside. Lucy follows.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: For the first time since the nightmare began, you can breathe without feeling trapped. You start running toward home. The road stretches ahead of you. No cars.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: No people. No movement. You pass the shops near the school. Their shutters are closed. Traffic lights blink over deserted intersections.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Your phone loses its signal completely. Lucy's phone does the same. Then you reach a familiar crossing. You stop. Across the road stands a bus.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Its doors are open.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The interior lights glow softly.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: A few students sit inside, staring straight ahead. You recognise their uniforms. They're students from your school. You run toward the bus.

blocks.speaker: Protagonist
blocks.text: "Hey! Help us!"

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Nobody responds. You reach the open doors.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Every student turns toward you at exactly the same time.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Their faces are pale and expressionless.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: At the back of the bus sits a girl wearing a school uniform.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Her hair falls across her shoulders. A small bracelet circles her wrist. You look at Lucy. Lucy is standing beside you.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The girl on the bus has the same face. The same eyes. The same clothes. Another Lucy.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The girl inside slowly raises her head. Then she smiles. The bus doors slam shut. The engine starts.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You watch as the vehicle drives away into the dark. Lucy doesn't move. You turn toward her. She is staring at her bracelet.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Her fingers tremble as she tries to pull it off. It won't come loose. She looks up at you.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: There's something I didn't tell you.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You wait.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: When I disappeared, I wasn't alone.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Her voice breaks.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "I saw someone standing in the road."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You feel the blood drain from your face.

blocks.speaker: Protagonist
blocks.text: "Who?"

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Lucy looks toward the direction the bus disappeared.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "You."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: The sky begins to roar again. The streetlights flicker.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: And every clock in the city stops at exactly 3:17. Lucy grips your hand.

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: "I think,

blocks.speaker: Lucy
blocks.text: we were never supposed to come back."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Behind you, the school bell rings. Once. Twice. Three times.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: Then the loudspeaker crackles to life.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: A voice speaks through the darkness.

blocks.speaker: Principal
blocks.text: "Attention, students."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: A pause.

blocks.speaker: Principal
blocks.text: "One student is still missing."

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: You turn toward the school. In an upstairs classroom window, someone is standing behind the glass. Watching you. It's you. Your past self.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: He raises one hand and presses it against the window. Then the lights go out.

blocks.speaker: Narrator
blocks.text: And somewhere in the darkness, you hear a door open. End.
